bullets.text: Machine Learning (ML) is a fast-growing area in technology and a subfield of Artificial Intelligence (AI).
ML systems learn patterns from data to make decisions or predictions, rather than being explicitly programmed.
Models improve over time with more data without needing reprogramming.
It's about teaching computers to learn from experience by providing data and letting them find patterns.

sections.heading: Ubiquity and Drivers of ML Growth

bullets.text: Machine learning is pervasive, used in Netflix recommendations, spam filters, virtual assistants, and fraud detection.
Its popularity stems from three major developments over the last decade.
Access to huge amounts of data (social media, web searches, GPS).
Increased computational power (modern hardware, GPUs).
Development of sophisticated algorithms for data insight extraction.
The most common type of ML, especially in industry applications.
Models are trained using labeled data, meaning each input has a correct output.
The goal is to learn input-output relationships to predict outputs for new, unseen inputs.
Example: Predicting house prices based on features and actual sale prices.
Problems are categorized into Regression (predicting continuous values) and Classification (predicting discrete labels).
Uses data without labeled outputs; only inputs are provided.
Algorithms discover patterns, relationships, or structures in the data independently.
Common application: Clustering, like grouping customers by buying behavior.
Another application: Dimensionality reduction (e.g., PCA) to simplify datasets with many features.
An agent learns by interacting with an environment, making decisions and receiving feedback.
Feedback comes as rewards or penalties, adjusting the agent's strategy.
Goal: Learn a policy to maximize total reward over time.
Examples: Training robots to walk, game-playing AI (AlphaGo), self-driving cars.
Data quality is crucial; noisy, biased, or incomplete data harms model performance.
Overfitting occurs when a model learns training data too well but fails on new data.
Ethical concerns are prominent, as biased data can lead to biased models with serious real-world consequences.
ML requires understanding data, context, and impact, not just algorithms.
Recap of ML definition, importance, three main types (supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement), and challenges.
Future lectures will delve deeper into each ML type, algorithms, and practical examples.
